last_attempts_log.asr_text: On the train, I open the For You page and see my followed topics first. I have only the ride to catch up, so I do not want to sort through unrelated stories. Google News uses topics and sources I follow. It can also use my past activity on Google services and YouTube. I can follow or unfollow topics, ask for more or less, and hide a source. These controls make the feed feel partly mine. I still worry an important story could be left out, but this quick start protects my morning time.

last_attempts_log.asr_text: Each time I scroll, I see familiar arguments and sources. I begin to wonder about stories outside that circle. I want to know why one article comes before another, but I cannot see all the signals behind the order, or how much control I have over the recommendations. Clicks, likes, shares, and search history can shape what appears. The service may also be tuned for engagement and advertising income. That makes me uneasy. A hidden order may be choosing what I notice first. I want to protect my chance to meet views I would not normally open.
Each morning, a phone lights up on a crowded train, a news page opens, and the first stories seem to know what the reader follows. There is only a short ride to work.
For one reader, this is a helpful shortcut. For another, the same screen raises a quiet question: what important story may be missing? The system is the same; the experience is not.

Both readers want the same thing: the feed shapes what they understand. Neither is wrong to care about that, but they protect different stakes. One wants a manageable morning and control, the other wants views outside the usual feed. The first can follow, hide, or change display levels. The second cannot reach the ranking rules, which may shape the view without showing how. This is an uneven process, not two equal controls.

The deeper question is not simply whether personalization helps or harms, it is who can shape the path to news and who can see that path. A feed may feel personal because it answers to a reader’s choices, while part of the decision stays out of view. That boundary is the real tension.
